item.title: Shirakawa-go: Japan's Famous UNESCO Gassho-Zukuri Village — Guide
item.description: Shirakawa-go is Japan’s most famous gassho-zukuri village and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, its steep, thatched-roof farmhouses, some more than 250 years old, designed to shed the region’s heavy winter snowfall and built without nails using a distinctive prayer-hands roof structure. Set amid rice paddies against a mountain backdrop in a remote valley, the village of Ogimachi is beautiful across every season, and a number of the historic farmhouses operate as guesthouses offering overnight farmhouse stays, letting visitors experience the interior and hospitality of these remarkable buildings first-hand.

item.title: Gokayama: UNESCO Gassho-Zukuri Village & Doburoku Sake Festival — Guide
item.description: Gokayama is a UNESCO World Heritage cluster of gassho-zukuri farmhouses, distinguished by their steep, thatched roofs designed to shed heavy mountain snowfall, sitting in a remote valley considerably quieter than its better-known counterpart Shirakawa-go across the prefectural border. Each autumn, the village of Kaminashi celebrates the harvest with the traditional Doburoku Festival, offering visitors a taste of unrefined doburoku sake alongside shrine rituals and folk performances rooted in the isolated valley’s centuries-old traditions.

item.title: Nikko Toshogu & Rinno-ji: Japan's Most Lavishly Decorated Shrine — Guide
item.description: Nikko Toshogu, the mausoleum of shogun Tokugawa Ieyasu who unified Japan and founded the Tokugawa shogunate, is the most lavishly decorated shrine in the country, its buildings covered in intricate gold leaf carvings, including the famous ‘see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil’ three wise monkeys. Together with the neighbouring Rinno-ji temple and Futarasan Shrine, it forms the ‘Shrines and Temples of Nikko’ UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the elaborate spring grand festival each May re-enacts a historic samurai procession honouring Ieyasu.

item.title: Shirakawa-go from Toyama: Visiting Japan's Famous Gassho-Zukuri Village — Guide
item.description: Shirakawa-go, Japan’s most famous UNESCO World Heritage gassho-zukuri village, is technically located just across the prefectural border in Gifu, but Toyama Station serves as one of the most convenient gateways for visiting, with direct highway buses running in around an hour. The village’s steep, thatched-roof farmhouses, some over 250 years old, are especially striking when illuminated during limited winter evening light-up events, and the surrounding rice paddies and mountain backdrop make it one of the most photographed rural landscapes in Japan.

item.title: Tomioka Silk Mill: Japan's UNESCO-Listed Industrial Pioneer — Guide
item.description: Tomioka Silk Mill, established in 1872 as Japan’s first government-run modern silk-reeling factory, played a pivotal role in Japan’s rapid industrialisation during the Meiji era, employing French engineering expertise alongside traditional Japanese wooden-frame construction techniques. Remarkably well preserved, the mill’s brick-and-timber cocoon warehouses and reeling plant were designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014, and the site’s annual autumn Silk Festival celebrates the region’s silk-producing heritage with demonstrations and local crafts.
